title: A photo from phone to phone
description: A photo becomes binary numbers at the camera sensor, is handled by transistor switches following software, crosses the internet as packets and is rebuilt as pixels.

facts.text: A digital camera's sensor is covered in light receptors, or pixels; light striking them induces an electric current that is translated into binary digits for storage.
During each clock cycle, billions of transistors, tiny switches, open and close inside a processor.
Software is the programs, the instructions that tell a computer's hardware what to do.
The internet is a network of networks: routers link local networks, and internet service providers link their routers to each other.
Packet switching breaks data into small packets that travel independently over any available route and are reassembled at the destination.
On a screen, an image is a grid of pixels, each a mix of red, green and blue light set by numbers.

title: What a bit is
description: A bit, short for binary digit, holds one choice between two alternatives, 1 or 0; in hardware a transistor on or off stores it. Tukey coined the word (1947); Shannon first printed it (1948).

facts.text: A bit, short for binary digit, is the unit of information given by one choice between two alternatives, written 1 or 0.
In a computer, a transistor switch stores a bit: on is 1 and off is 0.
John Tukey is credited with first using the word bit, a blend of binary and digit, for a unit of information, in a 1947 memo.
Claude Shannon's 1948 paper contains the first published use of the word bit.

title: Each bit doubles the patterns
description: Every added bit doubles the number of patterns: 1 bit 2, 2 bits 4, 3 bits 8, so a byte of 8 bits has 256.

facts.text: 1 bit gives 2 patterns (0, 1); 2 bits give 4 (00, 01, 10, 11); 3 bits give 8: each added bit doubles the number of patterns.
A byte is 8 bits, which can make 256 different patterns: doubling from 2 eight times gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256.

title: Kilo, mega, giga, tera
description: Storage sizes count bytes with the metric prefixes: kilo, mega, giga and tera mean a thousand, a million, a billion and a trillion, each step 1,000 times the last.

facts.text: Kilo, mega, giga and tera mean a thousand, a million, a billion and a trillion: each step up is 1,000 times the last.
One byte is enough to hold about one typed character, so a few dozen characters of plain text take a few dozen bytes.

title: How big a photo, a movie and a drive are
description: A 24.2-megapixel photo is about 73 MB raw and about 3.6 MB as JPEG; HD streaming uses up to 3 GB an hour; a 1 TB drive holds a trillion bytes.

facts.text: A 24.2-megapixel camera takes photos of 6,016 by 4,016 pixels, about 24 million pixels.
Stored at 3 bytes per pixel (one each for red, green and blue), a 24.2-megapixel photo takes about 72.6 million bytes, about 73 MB.
JPEG compression of 20 to 1 is easily done with practically invisible loss of quality, which would shrink a 73 MB photo to about 3.6 MB.
Netflix says streaming in high definition uses up to 3 GB per hour, so a two-hour film uses up to 6 GB.

title: Why a 1 TB drive shows 931 GB
description: Drive makers count a terabyte as 10^12 bytes; Windows counts a gigabyte as 1,073,741,824 bytes (1,024 cubed), so a 1 TB drive shows about 931 GB. No bytes are missing.

facts.text: A 1 TB drive holds 1,000,000,000,000 bytes; Windows counts a gigabyte as 1,073,741,824 bytes (1,024 × 1,024 × 1,024), so it shows the drive as about 931 GB.

title: ASCII: letters as numbers
description: ASCII (1963) gives letters, digits and punctuation standard numbers using 7 bits, so 128 characters; A is 65, and upper and lower case differ by one bit.

facts.text: ASCII, approved as an American standard in 1963, uses 7-bit binary numbers, so it can represent 128 different characters.
In ASCII, uppercase A is the number 65 and B is 66.
In ASCII, 1010000 is uppercase P and 1110000 is lowercase p: the two codes differ in a single bit.

title: Unicode and emoji
description: Unicode gives every character in every writing system a unique number, replacing hundreds of clashing encodings; emoji are Unicode numbers that each phone maker draws its own way.

facts.text: Before Unicode there were hundreds of character encodings, and they conflicted: two could use the same number for two different characters.
Unicode gives a unique number to every character, whatever the platform, program or language.
Unicode 18.0, released in September 2026, holds 172,808 characters.
UTF-8, a form of Unicode, is backward-compatible with ASCII: ASCII's numbers still work.
The Unicode Consortium standardizes emoji codes; a phone receives an emoji as a number and draws it, so its style can differ between device makers.

title: Pixels as three numbers
description: A digital image is a grid of pixels; each pixel mixes red, green and blue light, each a number from 0 to 255 (one byte), giving 16,777,216 possible colors.

facts.text: A digital image is a grid of pixels, each a small square of one color.
Each pixel's color is a mix of red, green and blue light, each set by a number from 0 (off) to 255 (full brightness), which fits in one byte.
Three values of 0 to 255 give 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216 possible colors.

title: Sound as samples
description: Digital audio measures the sound wave at equal time intervals and stores each sample as a binary number; CDs take 44,100 samples a second, more than twice the top of human hearing.

facts.text: Digital recording samples the sound wave at points spaced at equal time intervals and encodes each sampled point as a binary number.
CDs sample sound 44,100 times a second (44.1 kHz).
Sampling must happen more than twice as fast as the highest frequency to capture; hearing reaches about 20 kHz, so CD audio needed more than about 40 kHz, 40,000 samples a second.

title: AND, OR and NOT gates
description: A logic gate turns yes-or-no inputs into one yes-or-no output: AND needs all inputs 1, OR needs any, NOT flips its input. Gates are built from transistors.

facts.text: A logic gate takes yes-or-no inputs (1 or 0) and produces one output, working like a switch that passes or blocks electrical pulses.
An AND gate outputs 1 only when all its inputs are 1; an OR gate outputs 1 if any input is 1.
A NOT gate, or inverter, outputs the opposite of its input: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
Logic gate circuits are built from components such as transistors.
A lamp with two switches in series lights only when both are closed (AND); with two switches in parallel it lights when either is closed (OR).
Connected together, logic gates can carry out arithmetic.

title: Boolean algebra meets switches
description: Boole (1847, 1854) built an algebra of true and false, 1 and 0; Shannon's master's thesis used it to lay the theory of switching circuits, the basis of digital circuits.

facts.text: George Boole began the algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, in 1847 and 1854; it treats statements as true or false, written 1 and 0.
Claude Shannon's master's thesis, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, used Boolean algebra to lay the theoretical groundwork of digital circuits.

title: Adding in binary
description: Binary sums have four cases: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+0=1 and 1+1=10, where a 1 is carried to the next place, just as in decimal.

facts.text: Adding two bits has four cases: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 10, a 0 with a 1 carried to the next place.
In binary, 3 + 1 is 11 + 01: the carries ripple left twice and give 100, which is 4.

title: Half and full adders
description: A half adder is an exclusive-OR (sum) plus an AND (carry); a full adder also takes the carry in, and full adders chained carry to carry add numbers of any length.

facts.text: A half adder adds two bits: its sum is exclusive OR, 1 when exactly one input is 1, and its carry is AND, 1 only when both are 1.
A half adder's sum, (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B), is built from AND, OR and NOT gates.
A full adder adds three bits, two digits plus the carry from the place to its right; full adders chained, each carry feeding the next, add longer binary numbers.
A processor's arithmetic-logic unit does addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, plus logic operations such as comparing data.

title: The fetch, decode, execute cycle
description: The processor fetches the instruction at the program counter's address, decodes its binary pattern, executes it, then repeats; jumps change the counter.

facts.text: A processor fetches the instruction at the address in its program counter, decodes the instruction's binary pattern into fields with meanings, and executes the operation.
After a fetch, the program counter usually steps on to the next instruction; jumps and branches can change it to point somewhere else.
When one instruction is executed, the cycle begins again with the next.

title: The clock and gigahertz
description: A clock sends pulses at a fixed rate to regulate the cycle; gigahertz counts billions of cycles a second, so 3.2 GHz is 3.2 billion.

facts.text: A clock emitting pulses at a fixed, precise frequency regulates the fetch, decode and execute cycle.
Clock speed counts the cycles a processor runs per second in gigahertz: a 3.2 GHz processor runs 3.2 billion cycles a second.

title: Memory in layers
description: Memory runs from fast, expensive registers and SRAM cache on the CPU to denser, slower DRAM main memory and slower, cheaper nonvolatile storage, because main memory lags the CPU.

facts.text: DRAM main memory typically takes 20 to 80 nanoseconds to access data, while a processor arithmetic operation may take a nanosecond or less.
Memory is organized as a hierarchy, from fast, expensive registers in the processor to slower, cheaper nonvolatile storage.
A processor has a small number of registers, very fast memory holding the current instructions and the data they work on.
Cache is fast SRAM on the processor chip, up to several megabytes, holding frequently used instructions and data.
SRAM is fast but physically large; a chip the same size holds several times as much DRAM, which is slower.
Main memory made of DRAM loses its contents when the power is turned off; storage is nonvolatile and keeps them.

title: Why a small cache works
description: Programs repeat instructions in loops and use related data (locality of reference), so after values are copied into cache, many requests are served from it.

facts.text: Programs show locality of reference, repeating the same instructions in loops and using related data, so once values are copied into cache, requests can be served from it.

title: Same bits, different meanings
description: Bits carry no meaning by themselves: the bytes 72, 73, 33 spell HI! as text or make a shade of yellow as a color. Context, such as the file format, decides.

facts.text: The bytes 72, 73 and 33 spell HI! when read as ASCII text, and are a shade of yellow when read as red, green and blue; as plain numbers they sum to 178.
Context, such as the file format, decides whether a program reads the same bits as numbers, text or colors.

title: Jacquard's punched-card loom
description: From 1804 Jacquard's loom read interchangeable punched cards: a hole let a pin through to lift a warp thread, no hole kept it down, so a chain of cards wove any pattern.

facts.text: In 1804 Joseph-Marie Jacquard patented a loom controlled by interchangeable punched cards, so any pattern could be woven automatically.
In a Jacquard loom, pins pass through a card's holes and their hooks raise warp threads; where there is no hole, the pin is stopped and the thread stays down.
Charles Babbage adopted the Jacquard loom's punched cards for his proposed Analytical Engine.

title: Hollerith's census tabulator
description: The 1880 US census took until 1887 to tabulate. Hollerith's machine read a punched card per person: pins through holes dipped into mercury and closed circuits that advanced dials, and the 1890 count took six months.

facts.text: Tabulating the 1880 US census by hand was not finished until 1887.
Herman Hollerith's counting machine used punched cards, each holding one person's census data.
In Hollerith's tabulator, a pin that passed through a hole dipped into mercury, completing an electric circuit that advanced a counting dial.
With Hollerith's machines, the population count of the 1890 US census was completed in six months, ahead of schedule and under budget.
Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company, after mergers, was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.

title: Babbage's Analytical Engine
description: In the 1830s Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose machine programmed with Jacquard-style punched cards, with a store for numbers and a mill for arithmetic. It was never built.

facts.text: In the 1830s Charles Babbage conceived the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose calculating machine to be programmed with punched cards.
The Analytical Engine's design had a store to hold numbers, comparable to memory, and a separate mill to do the arithmetic, comparable to a processor.
The Analytical Engine was never built: the funding never came.

title: Lovelace: more than numbers
description: In her 1843 notes Ada Lovelace saw that the Analytical Engine might act on things besides number, such as music, because numbers can stand for symbols, letters and notes.

facts.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a translation of Luigi Menabrea's article on the Analytical Engine, with extensive notes of her own.
Lovelace wrote that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves.
Lovelace wrote that the engine might act upon other things besides number, and might compose elaborate pieces of music.
Lovelace saw that numbers could represent things other than quantities, such as letters, symbols and musical notes.

title: Turing's machine
description: In 1936 Turing described an abstract machine: a tape of squares holding symbols, a head that reads, writes and moves one square at a time, and a finite table of instructions and states.

facts.text: In 1936 Alan Turing described an abstract computing machine, now called the Turing machine.
A Turing machine has a tape divided into squares, as long as needed, each square blank or holding one symbol.
The machine's head reads, writes or erases the symbol on one square at a time and moves one square left or right.
At each moment a Turing machine is in one of a finite number of states, and a finite table of instructions says what it does next.

title: The universal machine
description: Turing's universal machine reads another machine's instructions from its tape and does what that machine would do. The Church-Turing thesis says it can compute everything humanly computable; it cannot be proved.

facts.text: Turing's universal machine, given another machine's instructions written on its tape, can do whatever that machine would do.
The Church-Turing thesis holds that everything humanly computable can be computed by a universal Turing machine.
The Church-Turing thesis can't be proved, because it matches an informal idea, computability, to a formal definition.

title: Programming ENIAC by hand
description: ENIAC, built 1943 to 1945 at Penn, had to be set up for each problem by connecting wires and setting switches, which took many days; then it ran at electronic speed.

facts.text: ENIAC was built from 1943 to 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania and revealed to the public in February 1946.
Setting ENIAC up for a new problem meant working out a configuration, then connecting wires and setting switches by hand, which took many days.
ENIAC took its instructions from plugboards, and once they were set, it ran at electronic speed.

title: The ENIAC Six
description: Six women, former human computers, programmed ENIAC from its diagrams without manuals; Jennings and Snyder devised the 1946 demonstration program. They went uncredited for decades and entered a hall of fame in 1997.

facts.text: ENIAC's first programmers were six women: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman.
Before programming ENIAC, the six had worked as human computers, calculating trajectories for the US Army.
The programmers were given ENIAC's wiring and logical diagrams but no manuals or programming languages, and worked out how its panels worked.
The trajectory program run at ENIAC's February 1946 demonstration was devised by Jean Jennings and Betty Snyder.
Published articles and photos of ENIAC featured only men, and the women programmers were not invited to the celebration dinner.
In 1997 the six ENIAC programmers were inducted into the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame.

title: The stored program
description: A stored-program computer keeps instructions in the same memory as its data (von Neumann and colleagues, 1945), so a program can be changed without rewiring: the birth of software.

facts.text: In a stored-program computer, the instructions and the data are kept together in the same memory.
The stored-program design was proposed by John von Neumann and colleagues in 1945, for the EDVAC computer.
Because a stored program is simply data in memory, it can be changed, moved or even produced by another program, with no rewiring.
Storing a computer's instructions in its memory was the birth of software, used by every computer since.

title: The Manchester Baby
description: On June 21, 1948 the Manchester Baby, built by Williams, Kilburn and Tootill, first ran a program from its electronic memory, a cathode-ray tube store.

facts.text: On June 21, 1948, the Manchester Baby became the first computer to run a program stored in its electronic memory.
The Baby was built at the University of Manchester by Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill.
The Baby's memory was a Williams-Kilburn tube, which stored bits on a cathode-ray tube.
The Baby's first program searched for the highest factor of a number.

title: The vacuum tube switch
description: Early electronic computers switched with vacuum tubes, whose heated cathodes used a lot of power and burned out: ENIAC had about 18,000 and lost one every day or two.

facts.text: ENIAC had about 18,000 vacuum tubes and lost one roughly every day or two.
A vacuum tube gets its electrons from a cathode heated to about 1,000°C or more, which takes significant power.
Vacuum tubes tend to burn out, mainly when their heated filaments fail.

title: The transistor
description: Bardeen and Brattain made the first transistor at Bell Labs in December 1947, in Shockley's group; all three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize. A small, cool, reliable on-off switch, it replaced tubes by the late 1950s.

facts.text: In December 1947 at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain made the first working transistor, from germanium.
Bardeen and Brattain worked in a solid-state physics group at Bell Labs organized by William Shockley.
Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the transistor effect.
A transistor can work as a switch: if current flows, the circuit is on, and if not, it is off.
Transistors are small, give off little heat, are highly reliable and use little power, which let complex circuits shrink.
By the late 1950s, transistors had replaced vacuum tubes in many uses.

title: The integrated circuit
description: Wiring thousands of separate parts was the obstacle to smaller circuits. The integrated circuit builds transistors and their connections on one piece of semiconductor; Kilby (1958) and Noyce (1959) are both credited.

facts.text: As electronic systems grew, wiring together thousands of separate transistors and other parts became the main obstacle to making circuits smaller.
An integrated circuit builds transistors, other components and the connections between them on one thin piece of semiconductor, usually silicon.
Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958 and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959 independently developed the integrated circuit; both are credited.
Noyce's integrated circuit connected its parts with metal lines laid on top of the silicon, doing away with loose wire connections.

title: Moore's prediction
description: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted chip components would double every year, to about 65,000 by 1975; in 1975 he revised it to every two years. It was an observation that became an industry target, not a law of physics.

facts.text: In 1965, in Electronics magazine, Gordon Moore predicted the number of components on a chip would double every year, reaching about 65,000 by 1975.
In 1975, as growth began to slow, Moore revised his forecast to a doubling every two years.
Moore's law is an observation, not a law of physics; meeting Moore's timetable became a goal for engineers.

title: The computer comes home
description: The 1971 microprocessor put a processor on one chip, making personal computers affordable: the 1975 Altair kit with switches and lights, then the preassembled Apple II, PET and TRS-80 of 1977.

facts.text: Intel's 4004 of 1971, the first microprocessor, put a complete general-purpose processor on one chip, with 2,300 transistors.
A powerful microprocessor on a single chip made affordable personal computers possible.
In January 1975 Popular Electronics ran a cover story on the Altair 8800, a computer kit from MITS, and orders flooded in.
The Altair was built around Intel's 8080 microprocessor.
The basic Altair had no keyboard or screen: only toggle switches and binary lights for input and output.
In 1977 three preassembled, mass-produced personal computers arrived: the Apple II, the Commodore PET and the TRS-80.
The Apple II was sold complete, with a keyboard, case and power supply.

title: The IBM PC standard
description: IBM's 1981 PC used off-the-shelf parts, Intel's 8088 and Microsoft's MS-DOS, and published its design; rivals built IBM compatibles, and the design became the industry standard.

facts.text: IBM unveiled the IBM PC in August 1981, with Intel's 8088 processor and an operating system from Microsoft, later called MS-DOS.
IBM built the PC from off-the-shelf parts and published a technical reference describing it.
Other companies built IBM-compatible computers with Intel processors and MS-DOS, and the PC's design became an industry standard.

title: Smartphones and app stores
description: A smartphone runs an operating system that installs other software. The iPhone (2007) brought fingertip touchscreens; the App Store (2008) and Android (2008, open source, many makers) opened phones to outside apps.

facts.text: A smartphone is a mobile phone with an operating system that lets other software be installed, for web browsing, email, music, video and more.
Apple announced the iPhone in January 2007, and it went on sale in the US in June 2007.
The iPhone was worked with fingertips on a touchscreen, rather than a stylus or physical keys.
Apple opened the App Store on July 10, 2008, with 500 apps, letting outside developers offer software for the phone.
The first phone running Google's Android, the T-Mobile G1, went on sale in October 2008.
Android is a free, open-source system that supports third-party apps and is used by many phone manufacturers.

title: The phone as the main computer
description: In October 2016 phones and tablets passed desktops in worldwide web use; by 2025, 91% of US adults owned a smartphone (35% in 2011) and 16% were smartphone-only internet users.

facts.text: In October 2016, mobile and tablet devices accounted for 51.3% of worldwide web use, passing desktops at 48.7%.
In 2025, 91% of US adults owned a smartphone, up from 35% in 2011.
In 2025, 16% of US adults were smartphone-only internet users: they had a smartphone but no home broadband.

title: Each era's switch
description: Computing history can be read by its switch: pins through punched holes closing circuits, then vacuum tubes, then transistors, then transistors built into integrated circuits.

facts.text: Computing's basic switch changed over time: pins closing circuits through punched holes, then vacuum tubes, then transistors, then transistors built into chips.

title: Spell out every step
description: A computer runs simple, mechanical operations with no insight, so a program must break a task into steps defined precisely for every case; everyday language is too loose, as a units mix-up that lost Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999 showed.

facts.text: Stanford's CS101 sums up computers as "Powerful + Stupid": billions of operations a second, each simple and mechanical, like adding or comparing two numbers, with no insight.
A computer needs a human to tell it what to do: programmers break a solution down into instructions simple enough for the computer to follow.
Computer scientist Donald Knuth lists definiteness as a feature of every algorithm: each step must be precisely defined, its action spelled out unambiguously for each case.

Knuth notes that a recipe lacks definiteness: "Add a dash of salt" doesn't say exactly how much or where, which is why programs are written in formal languages where every statement has a definite meaning.
Code's syntax must be followed rigidly: something any person could understand still won't run unless it fits the computer's exact rules.

Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because of a failure to use metric units: a ground software file produced thruster data in English units, while the trajectory software that used that data expected metric, so the trajectory calculations sent it too close to Mars.
The last contact with Mars Climate Orbiter was on 23 September 1999, and an investigation found it burned up in Mars's atmosphere.

title: Machine code: the processor's own language
description: Only machine code runs on a processor. It is hardwired into each family of processors, such as x86, so one family's machine code does not run on another, and each instruction is a tiny operation a few bytes long.

facts.text: Only machine code actually runs on a processor; code written in a programming language is translated into machine code, and that translation is what runs.
A processor's machine code is hardwired into its design, and each family of compatible processors, such as Intel's x86, has its own machine code that other families can't run.
Each machine code instruction is extremely simple, such as adding two numbers or testing whether a number is zero, and takes just a few bytes; a big program is millions of them.

title: Compilers, interpreters and bytecode
description: Source code reaches machine code in different ways: a compiler translates it ahead of time into a machine code file; an interpreter runs it directly, as Python does via bytecode on a virtual machine; browsers compile JavaScript just in time.

facts.text: A compiler translates a program ahead of time: Firefox's source code, for example, is compiled into Firefox.exe, a file made mostly of machine code bytes.
With only a compiled program file you can run the program but not change it; the human-readable source code is what programmers edit.
No single machine code instruction can print, so one line of source code, like a print command, is translated into many machine instructions.
Python is interpreted, so its source files run directly with no separate executable; its standard interpreter first compiles code into bytecode, which a virtual machine runs.
Just-in-time (JIT) compilers turn code into machine code while a program runs, and all major browsers use JavaScript engines with built-in JIT compilers.

title: Why there are many languages
description: Languages are built for different jobs and trade different costs: C, made for writing Unix, stays close to the machine and is efficient; JavaScript runs in every major browser; Python is easy to write but, being interpreted, generally runs more slowly.

facts.text: Dennis Ritchie turned the B language into C at Bell Labs during 1971 to 1973 as a language for writing Unix, and in summer 1973 the Unix kernel was rewritten in C.
C's types and operations mirror those of real machines, which made it efficient enough to replace assembly language for writing systems.
Ritchie summed up his language this way: "C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success."
JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich while he worked at Netscape, and it arrived in the Netscape Navigator 2.0 browser in September 1995.
JavaScript is primarily used in web browsers, where it changes a page's content, fetches data from servers and draws graphics.
Guido van Rossum started Python over the 1989 Christmas holidays and posted it publicly in February 1991; it is a high-level, general-purpose language with a large standard library.
Interpreted languages typically have a shorter write-and-fix cycle than compiled ones, but their programs generally run more slowly.

title: Variables remember values
description: A variable is a name that refers to a value, so a program can keep and update a value it can't predict in advance through a name chosen ahead of time.

facts.text: A variable is a named reference to a value, so a value that can't be predicted in advance can still be reached through a name chosen ahead of time.

title: Choosing with if, repeating with loops
description: A conditional runs instructions only when a condition holds; a loop repeats instructions until a condition is met. At the machine level, an if skips instructions and a loop jumps back to an earlier one.

facts.text: A conditional runs an instruction or set of instructions if a condition is met, and other instructions if it isn't.
A loop is a sequence of instructions repeated until a condition is met, such as a counter reaching a set number.
At the machine level, a loop is an instruction that jumps back to an earlier point, and an if is one that skips over instructions when a condition is true.

title: Binary search
description: Binary search checks the middle of a sorted list and discards the half that can't hold the target, again and again, so a million sorted items need at most about 20 steps and doubling the list adds only one.

facts.text: Binary search goes to the middle of a sorted list, asks whether the target is before or after it, throws away the other half, and repeats on what's left.
Binary search only works on a sorted list, not an unsorted one.
A linear search checks items one by one, so in the worst case it needs as many steps as there are items: a million for a million.
For a million items in a sorted list, binary search needs at most about 20 steps; for two million, only about 21.
Doubling the size of the list adds only one more step to binary search.

title: How an algorithm's steps grow
description: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's steps grow with its input: doubling the input adds one step for O(log n), doubles the work for O(n), quadruples it for O(n squared), and some problems, like checking every traveling-salesperson route, grow far faster.

facts.text: Computer scientists describe an algorithm's efficiency with big O notation: the order of how its running time grows with the size of the input, n, with constant factors dropped, so searching two pages at a time is still O(n).
When the data doubles, an O(log n) algorithm needs one extra step, an O(n) one needs twice the steps, and an O(n x n) one needs four times the steps.
Linear search is O(n) and binary search is O(log n).
A simple sort such as selection sort makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n squared).
The traveling salesperson problem asks for the cheapest way to visit every city in a set and return to where you started.
A round trip through n cities has (n-1)!/2 different tours: 12 for 5 cities and 181,440 for 10, a growth that rules out checking tours one by one.

title: Sharing one processor
description: The operating system time-shares the processor: a timer interrupt returns control every few milliseconds, a context switch saves and restores registers and the program counter, and multicore chips truly run programs at once.

facts.text: An operating system shares one processor among many programs by running one for a little while, then another, and so on.
At start-up, the operating system sets a hardware timer to raise an interrupt every few milliseconds; when it fires, the running program is halted and the operating system's handler runs.
Without a timer interrupt, if a program gets stuck in an endless loop and never gives up the processor, the only recourse is to reboot.
In a context switch, the operating system saves the running program's registers and program counter and restores the saved ones of the next program, so each resumes where it stopped.
A program waiting on a disk can be blocked for milliseconds or longer, so the scheduler runs another program on the processor meanwhile.
Multicore chips pack several processor cores onto one chip and are now common in desktops, laptops and phones, but a typical program uses only one core unless rewritten to run in parallel.

title: How a file system tracks files
description: In many file systems, a directory pairs each file name with an inode number; the inode records the file's size and where its data blocks are; a bitmap marks each block free (0) or in use (1).

facts.text: In many file systems, a directory is a list of entries pairing each file's name with an inode number.
A file's inode records information about it, including its size and where its blocks of data are on the drive.
A file system can track free space with a bitmap: one bit per block, 0 if the block is free and 1 if it is in use.

title: Why deleted files can come back
description: Deleting usually removes a file's name link and marks its space free without erasing the data, which stays until overwritten and can often be recovered; SSDs often wipe freed blocks via TRIM, and real sanitising means overwriting or deleting encryption keys.

facts.text: Deleting a file removes the link between its name and its inode; only when no names still point to it does the file system free the inode and data blocks.
A deleted file is typically not erased: the record pointing to it is marked deleted, and its space is treated as free, which the operating system can overwrite at any time.
Until it is overwritten, data from a deleted file can often be recovered with forensic and recovery tools.

On solid-state drives, a command called TRIM lets the operating system say which areas are no longer needed, and the drive's background garbage collection can then clear them, destroying deleted data.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warns that hitting Delete isn't enough to clear a device: overwrite all its memory or, on encrypted devices, use a factory reset that deletes the encryption keys.

title: The 1947 moth and the word bug
description: On 9 September 1947 a moth found in the Harvard Mark II's relays was taped into the log as the 'first actual case of bug being found'; the word bug for a fault already dated to Edison's day.

facts.text: On 9 September 1947, a team found a moth caught between the relay contacts of the Harvard Mark II in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and taped it into the logbook as the "First actual case of bug being found."
Grace Hopper was present when the moth was found and later made the incident famous in her many talks.
Calling a technical fault a bug was already in use long before 1947, going back to Thomas Edison in the 1800s.

title: Ariane 5 and the number too big to fit
description: Ariane 5's first flight in 1996 was lost when software reused from Ariane 4 converted a 64-bit value into a 16-bit integer that could not hold it; the identical backup failed the same way. A fixed number of bits can only hold so much.

facts.text: On 4 June 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket veered off its flight path, broke up and exploded about 40 seconds after its flight sequence began.

The inquiry board found Ariane 5 lost its guidance and attitude information 37 seconds after the main engine ignition sequence began, due to errors in the software of its inertial reference system, the unit that measures which way the rocket points and moves.
Ariane 5's inertial reference software, practically the same as Ariane 4's, converted a 64-bit floating-point number into a 16-bit signed integer, and the value was too large to fit.
The value was far higher than expected because Ariane 5's early trajectory gave much higher horizontal velocity than Ariane 4's.
Ariane 5's backup inertial reference system, identical in hardware and software, had already failed for the same reason.
Two bytes, 16 bits, give 65,536 combinations; a number stored in a fixed number of bits overflows when it runs out of bits, because there is nowhere left to carry.

title: Why testing can't prove a program correct
description: There are far too many possible inputs to test them all: Dijkstra reckoned that trying every multiplication on a 27-bit machine would take about 30,000 years, so testing can show bugs are present but never that they are absent.

facts.text: Edsger Dijkstra noted that his university's computer, with 27-bit words, had 2 to the power 54 possible multiplications; at 2 to the power 14 a second, trying each once would take about 30,000 years.
Dijkstra drew the moral: "program testing can be used very effectively to show the presence of bugs but never to show their absence."

title: Local networks, switches and routers
description: A LAN links the devices in one building; Ethernet has been its most common design since the mid-1970s. Switches link devices inside a network; routers link networks.

facts.text: A local area network (LAN) connects computers within a building or a small group of buildings.
Ethernet, originally developed at Xerox PARC, has been the most common LAN design since the mid-1970s.
A switch connects the devices within one network; a router connects networks to each other and to the internet, directing packets toward their destination.

title: MAC addresses and how a switch learns
description: Each network card has a 48-bit MAC address; a switch learns which port each address is behind and forwards frames only there, flooding when the destination is unknown.

facts.text: An Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes), hard-coded into read-only memory on the network card, and identifies devices on the local network, though software can change the address a device actually uses.
A switch learns by noting each incoming frame's source MAC address and the port it arrived on, and records them in its MAC address table.
If a frame's destination MAC address is in its table, a switch sends it out that one port; if not, out every port except the one it came in on.

title: IP addresses and IPv4 notation
description: Every device directly on the internet has an IP address, and every packet carries a source and destination address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255, about 4.3 billion in all.

facts.text: Every device directly connected to the internet has an IP address.
The Internet Protocol (IP) was specified in 1981, and every IP packet's header carries a source address and a destination address.
An IPv4 address is 32 bits, usually written as four 8-bit parts in decimal, each from 0 to 255, separated by periods, such as 128.9.0.32.
IPv4's 32-bit addresses allow 4,294,967,296 unique addresses, about 4.3 billion.

title: Running out of IPv4, and IPv6
description: IANA gave its last free IPv4 blocks to the five regional registries on February 3, 2011. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, a 39-digit number of them.

facts.text: On February 3, 2011, IANA handed the last blocks of its free IPv4 pool to the five regional internet registries, which distribute addresses in their regions.
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, 96 bits more than IPv4's 32, allowing 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456 addresses: a 39-digit number.

title: How DNS turns names into addresses
description: DNS replaced a single HOSTS.TXT file. A resolver turns a name into an IP address, following referrals from a root server to the TLD servers to the domain's own name servers.

facts.text: Before DNS, host names and addresses were kept by one office in a single file, HOSTS.TXT, that every computer copied; the network's growth made that unworkable.
The Domain Name System (DNS) turns a domain name into the IP address a computer uses to reach it; a browser hands the question to a program called a resolver.
The name example.com is reserved for use as an example in documentation.
A resolver with no saved answer asks a root server, which refers it to the .com servers, which refer it to the domain's own name servers, which give the address.

title: Root servers and DNS caching
description: Thirteen named root servers, run by twelve organizations from more than 2,000 machines, start every uncached lookup; resolvers cache answers so most lookups never reach them.

facts.text: The 13 named root servers, a to m, are run by 12 independent organizations using more than 2,000 machines around the world (2026).
Resolvers keep a cache of answers they looked up recently and check it before asking any server; this caching is critical for DNS to work at scale.

title: Hop-by-hop routing
description: Each router looks up a packet's destination IP address in its routing table and sends it one hop to the next router; networks share reachability with BGP.

facts.text: Each router chooses only the next hop for a packet, by looking up its destination address in the router's routing table.
Between the separate networks that make up the internet, routers use BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) to exchange which addresses each network can reach.

title: Time to Live and traceroute
description: Every packet carries an 8-bit Time to Live that each router lowers; at zero the packet is discarded, which stops loops. Traceroute uses this to reveal each hop.

facts.text: Every IP packet carries an 8-bit Time to Live (at most 255); each router must lower it by at least one and discard the packet at zero, notifying the sender.
The Time to Live's hop limit keeps routing problems from making packets loop through the network forever.
Traceroute sends a packet with a Time to Live of 1, then 2, and so on; each router that discards one reports back, revealing the path hop by hop.

title: The TCP handshake
description: TCP opens a connection with SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK, agreeing on starting sequence numbers; UDP skips all of this and guarantees nothing.

facts.text: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) opens a connection with a three-way handshake: SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK, which sets each side's starting sequence number.
UDP is connectionless and uses minimal protocol machinery: no handshake, no resending, and no guaranteed delivery; programs needing reliable, ordered delivery should use TCP.

title: How TCP makes delivery reliable
description: IP promises nothing, so TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges the next byte expected, uses checksums and resends data not acknowledged before a timeout.

facts.text: IP makes no delivery guarantee: packets may arrive damaged, duplicated, out of order or not at all, and the layers above must supply reliability.
TCP gives every byte a sequence number; an acknowledgment names the next byte expected, confirming all before it, and the numbers expose duplicates.
TCP detects lost data with sequence numbers and damaged data with checksums, and resends data not acknowledged before a retransmission timer runs out.

title: The four internet layers
description: The internet stacks four protocol layers, application, transport, internet and link, each doing one job; the OSI model slices the same work into seven.

facts.text: The internet's host requirements (1989) describe four protocol layers: application, transport (TCP and UDP), internet (IP) and link.
The transport layer carries data end to end between programs; IP carries it from the source computer to the destination computer; the link layer handles the directly connected network.
The OSI model, set out by the International Organization for Standardization, divides network communication into seven layers.
The internet's application layer combines the jobs of the OSI model's top two layers, presentation and application.

title: Encapsulation: headers in headers
description: Sending, each layer wraps what it gets with its own header (segment, packet, frame); receiving, each layer strips its counterpart's header and passes the rest up.

facts.text: Sending data, each layer adds its own header: TCP makes a segment with ports, ordering information and a checksum; IP adds addresses; the link layer adds a header and an error-check footer to make a frame.
On arrival, each layer strips off the header added by its counterpart on the sending computer and passes the rest up.

title: How fiber guides light
description: A fiber keeps light in a glass core by reflecting it off cladding with a lower refractive index; data travels as pulses of light, boosted by optical amplifiers on long links.

facts.text: Light going from a higher to a lower refractive index can reflect back instead of escaping; a fiber keeps light in a glass core wrapped in cladding of lower refractive index.
The core of a long-distance optical fiber is typically about 10 micrometers across, thinner than a human hair.
Optical fiber carries data as pulses of light through hair-thin glass strands, turning electrical signals into light.
Even pure fiber dims the signal slightly, so long links use optical amplifiers that boost the light without converting it to electricity.

title: Kao and the purity of glass
description: In 1966 Charles Kao, with George Hockham, showed that impurities in glass caused the loss; pure glass could carry light over 100 km instead of 20 m. He shared the 2009 Nobel Prize.

facts.text: In 1966 Charles Kao, with George Hockham, showed that impurities in the glass, rather than flaws in the fiber, were the main cause of lost light.
Kao calculated that fiber of the purest glass could carry light signals over 100 kilometers, compared with only 20 meters for the fibers of the 1960s.
Kao aimed for 1 percent of the light to remain after 1 kilometer of fiber; today about 95 percent remains.
Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on transmitting light in fibers for optical communication.

title: Private address blocks
description: IANA reserved three private blocks (including 192.168) that any network may reuse; they are unique only inside their network, and using them conserves public IPv4 addresses.

facts.text: IANA reserved three blocks for private networks: 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255.
Private addresses can be used without asking a registry, so many networks reuse them, but each is unique only inside its own network and can't be reached directly from the internet.
Using private addresses where global uniqueness isn't needed conserves public IPv4 addresses and lengthens the life of the address space.

title: Network address translation
description: A home router maps each private address and port to its one public address and a port it picks, keeping a table so replies get back; sessions normally start from inside.

facts.text: NAT with port translation maps each private address and port to the router's single public address and a port it assigns, so many devices share one public address.
A TCP header carries a 16-bit source port and a 16-bit destination port.
In traditional NAT, sessions normally start from inside the private network; sessions from outside need a fixed mapping set up in advance.

title: Last-mile links
description: The last mile links a home to its provider: DSL over phone lines, cable over TV coax, fiber to the home, fixed wireless, mobile broadband or satellite.

facts.text: The last mile is the link connecting a customer's home or business to the local network provider.
DSL (digital subscriber line) carries data over a copper telephone line while the line is still used for phone calls, without disrupting either.
Cable internet uses the same coaxial cables that carry TV pictures and sound.
Fiber to the home runs optical fiber directly to the building, and fiber carries data much faster than DSL or cable.
Fixed wireless sends data from a local antenna to a fixed home or business; mobile broadband reaches people on the move; satellite serves remote, sparsely populated areas.

title: Geostationary and low-orbit satellites
description: Geostationary satellites orbit 35,786 km up, matching Earth's spin so three cover the Earth, but the long trip adds lag; low-orbit satellites are closer but need big constellations.

facts.text: A geostationary satellite orbits 35,786 km above the equator, matching Earth's rotation so it stays over one spot; three can cover the Earth.
Because data must travel so far up to a geostationary satellite and back down, its users can see more lag than with other kinds of internet link.
Low Earth orbit is below 2,000 km; satellites there move across the sky, so hundreds to thousands are needed for steady coverage, and the shorter trip means less lag.

title: One request, start to finish
description: Loading a site by name takes a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake, layered headers, NAT, hop-by-hop routing and light in fiber; completeness comes from TCP at the two ends.

facts.text: Before a browser can contact a website by name, a resolver must look up the site's IP address through DNS.

title: Request and response
description: The web runs on HTTP: the browser always starts by sending a request (usually GET for a page), and the server answers with a response that opens with a status code such as 200 or 404.

facts.text: HTTP is a client-server protocol: the browser always initiates, sending a request, and the server answers with a response.
To fetch a resource such as a web page, the browser typically sends a GET request.
An HTTP response carries a status code: 200 (OK) means the request succeeded; 404 (Not Found) means the server cannot find what was requested.

title: A web that forgets
description: HTTP is stateless: no link between two requests, so each must carry everything needed. Fielding (2000) explains the choice: servers free resources and scale, at the cost of repeated data.

facts.text: HTTP is stateless: there is no link between two requests, even two in a row on the same connection, so the server does not remember the first when the second arrives.

In Roy Fielding's 2000 description of the web's architecture, each request must carry all the information needed to understand it, so servers keep no session state; they can free resources at once, which helps them scale and recover from partial failures.
The price of statelessness is repetition: each request resends information the server could otherwise have remembered.

title: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
description: A page arrives as instructions: HTML for structure and meaning, CSS for style, JavaScript for behavior. The browser fetches the HTML, then requests each file it refers to.

facts.text: HTML is the markup language that structures a page's content and gives it meaning: headings, paragraphs, tables, embedded images and video.
CSS is a language of style rules for a page: colors, fonts and layout such as columns.
JavaScript makes a page dynamic: it updates content, controls media and animates images.
To show a page, the browser first fetches the HTML document, then makes more requests for the scripts, CSS and images it refers to.

title: Why pages are sent as instructions
description: Because a page is instructions rather than a picture, it can lay itself out for any screen (responsive design) and screen readers can announce its structure.

facts.text: Responsive web design lets one page adapt its layout to any screen, whether it is viewed on a phone, tablet, television or watch.
Screen readers use a page's HTML to announce what is a heading and what is a paragraph, and let users jump from heading to heading.

title: Cookies give the web a memory
description: A cookie is a small piece of data a server sends and the browser returns with later requests, letting a stateless site tie requests into a session: sign-ins, carts, preferences.

facts.text: A cookie is a small piece of data a server sends to your browser; the browser stores it and sends it back to the same server with later requests.
Cookies are used for session management (sign-ins, shopping carts), personalization (language, theme) and tracking.
HTTP is stateless, but cookies allow stateful sessions: each request carries the cookie, so the server can link requests into one session.

title: Third-party cookies
description: A cookie from a domain other than the one in the address bar is third-party; a tracker embedded on many sites receives it on each and can profile your browsing. Safari and Firefox limit them by default.

facts.text: A cookie whose domain matches the site in the address bar is first-party; one from a different domain is third-party, often set by content embedded in the page.
A third-party server embedded on many sites receives its cookie from the same browser on each, so it can build a profile of a person's browsing history and habits.
Browser makers know people dislike this tracking: Safari and Firefox limit third-party cookies by default, and Firefox gives each site its own separate cookie jar.

title: Why renting computing wins
description: The cloud swaps buying computers up front for metered, elastic capacity that follows demand, and providers gain economies of scale by pooling machines across many customers.

facts.text: The cloud lets an organization replace capital investment in computers with operating expenses that follow actual use, and can lower the up-front cost of launching new services.
Rapid elasticity: cloud capacity can be added and released quickly, sometimes automatically, as demand rises and falls, and to the customer it can seem unlimited.
Measured service: cloud use such as storage, processing and bandwidth is metered, monitored and reported.
Cloud providers pool their machines to serve many customers, gaining economies of scale.

title: What the cloud costs in control
description: Moving to a public cloud transfers control over data and systems to the provider and creates dependence on it, while the customer stays accountable for security and privacy.

facts.text: Moving to a public cloud transfers control over data and systems to the provider, leaving the customer dependent on the provider's cooperation for tasks such as monitoring and incident response.
An organization that moves to a public cloud remains accountable for the security and privacy of what it outsources.

title: Data centers turn power into heat
description: Most of a data center's electricity ends up as heat that must be removed; PUE (total facility energy over IT energy) scores the overhead, about 1.6 on average (DOE, 2024).

facts.text: Most of the electricity a data center uses ends up as heat, which has to be carried away.
US data centers used about 176 TWh of electricity in 2023, about 4.4% of all US electricity, according to a 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report.

PUE (power usage effectiveness) is a data center's total energy divided by the energy used by its IT equipment; 1.0 would mean every watt goes to computing and none to cooling, lighting or other loads.
The US Department of Energy's 2024 guide puts an average data center's PUE at about 1.6, with some very efficient ones below 1.1; at 1.6, each watt of computing needs about 0.6 watts of overhead.

title: Why climate and water shape where data centers go
description: Cool outside air can replace chillers (free cooling), and cooling towers evaporate water in proportion to the heat, so climate and water help decide where data centers are built.

facts.text: When outside air is cooler than the air leaving the servers, a data center can use it instead of mechanical chillers, called free cooling; many data centers in cool climates use only this kind of cooling.
Cooling towers shed a data center's heat by evaporating water, so their water use rises with the heat the IT equipment produces.

title: Bandwidth versus latency
description: Bandwidth is how much data a connection carries per second; latency is how long data takes to arrive, usually measured as a round trip. Pages need many round trips, so latency adds up.

facts.text: Bandwidth is how much information can pass through a connection in a given time, measured in bits per second, such as megabits per second (Mbps).
Latency is the time data takes to travel from one computer to another, generally measured as a round trip.
Websites involve many requests, since the HTML asks for CSS, scripts and media files, so high latency adds delay to each one.

title: Distance sets a delay no plan removes
description: Light in fiber takes about 4.9 microseconds per km, so New York to London costs about 28 ms one way. More bandwidth can't shorten that; engineers cut round trips and move data closer.

facts.text: Light takes about 3.34 microseconds per kilometer in a vacuum but about 4.9 microseconds per kilometer in optical fiber, because glass slows it.
New York to London is about 5,585 km; light in fiber needs about 28 milliseconds to cover it one way, about 56 milliseconds for a round trip.
Latency, not bandwidth, is the performance bottleneck for most websites; more bandwidth cannot beat the speed of light, so engineers make fewer round trips and move data closer to users.

title: Copies near you: content delivery networks
description: A CDN keeps copies of data on servers in many places and answers from the nearest; Netflix's Open Connect places servers inside internet providers and fills them off-peak with what viewers will likely watch.

facts.text: A content delivery network (CDN) is a group of servers in many locations that store copies of data, so each request is answered by a server close to the user; this makes service fast and less affected by heavy traffic.
Netflix's own CDN, Open Connect, offers internet providers Netflix servers to install inside their networks, free of charge to qualifying providers, to keep video close to viewers.
Because Netflix can predict what its members will watch and when, it copies most new content onto those servers during off-peak hours.
Each Open Connect server installed inside a provider takes a substantial amount of Netflix traffic off the links between that provider and other networks.

title: Lossless and lossy compression
description: Lossless compression removes repetition and can be reversed exactly (run-length encoding, Zip); lossy compression, like JPEG, discards detail people barely notice, fine for images and voice but not text.

facts.text: Lossless compression can be reversed to give back the original data exactly; lossy compression loses some detail or introduces small errors.
Run-length encoding replaces a run of repeated items with a count and one copy of the item.
Zip files use lossless compression.
Lossy compression can be acceptable for images and voice, where small errors spread over scattered spots are hard to notice, but text needs exactness.
JPEG compression is lossy: it averages out color variation and discards what the human eye cannot see.

title: Video stores the changes
description: Video compression, such as MPEG, stores only the slight differences between successive frames instead of every frame whole.

facts.text: Video can be compressed by storing only the slight differences between successive frames, as MPEG standards do; where little moves, little needs storing.

title: How one change took Facebook offline
description: On October 4, 2021, a maintenance command cut Facebook's backbone; its DNS servers then withdrew their BGP route announcements and became unreachable, taking Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp down for about six hours.

facts.text: On October 4, 2021, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp were down worldwide for about six hours; Meta called it an error of its own making.

During routine maintenance, a command meant to assess Facebook's backbone capacity accidentally took down every connection in its backbone network, cutting its data centers off from each other and the internet; a bug in an audit tool failed to stop it.
DNS is the internet's address book: it translates names typed into browsers into the IP addresses of servers.
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how networks on the internet exchange information about which addresses they can reach.
Facebook's DNS servers were built to withdraw their BGP route announcements if they could not reach the data centers; they did, so they became unreachable even though they were still running.

title: Why the fix took hours
description: The Facebook outage also knocked out internal tools, and engineers had to reach secure data centers in person; Meta credited practice drills with helping it restore service carefully.

facts.text: The outage also knocked out many internal tools Meta's engineers used day to day, which made diagnosing and fixing the problem harder.
Engineers had to go to the data centers in person, where buildings designed to be hard to get into, and hardware designed to be hard to modify, slowed the repair.
Meta said practice drills for large failures helped it bring services back online and manage the returning load carefully.

title: One web page, start to finish
description: Loading a page: DNS lookup for the IP address, a TCP handshake (plus TLS for HTTPS), a GET for the HTML, more requests for its files, then parsing, layout and painting into pixels.

facts.text: Once it has the server's IP address, the browser opens a connection with a TCP three-way handshake, and for HTTPS a TLS handshake that verifies the server and sets up encryption.
With the connection open, the browser sends an HTTP GET request, most often for an HTML file.
The browser parses the HTML into the DOM and the CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree and computes the layout of every visible element.
In the last step, painting, the browser converts each box calculated in layout into actual pixels on the screen.

title: Every system has holes; zero-days
description: All systems contain vulnerabilities, some unknown even to their makers; an attack on a flaw the maker did not yet know about is a zero-day.

facts.text: All systems contain vulnerabilities, flaws an attacker could use, including some the software's maker does not yet know exist.
A zero-day attack exploits a previously unknown vulnerability; the name means the maker has had zero days to fix it.

title: The race to patch
description: Patches fix known flaws, but attackers keep targeting unpatched machines for months or years, as WannaCry showed in 2017; so install updates promptly and automatically.

facts.text: A patch is a software update that fixes security vulnerabilities.
Attackers may target vulnerabilities for months or even years after updates that fix them are available.
Microsoft released a fix for the flaw on March 14, 2017; the WannaCry ransomware, released on May 12, 2017, hit computers that had not applied it.
In England, at least 81 of 236 NHS trusts were affected by WannaCry, and the infected organisations had unpatched or unsupported Windows.
CISA advises installing updates as soon as possible and turning on automatic updates.

title: Storing a hash, not the password
description: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length output that cannot feasibly be reversed; sites store the hash and compare hashes at login. Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible with a key.

facts.text: A hash function turns input of any length into a fixed-length output, and it is computationally infeasible to work back from an output to an input.
A well-run site stores only the hash of your password; at login it hashes what you type and compares the result with the stored hash.
Hashing is one-way, with nothing to decrypt; encryption is two-way, so anyone with the key can turn it back into readable text.

title: Salted, deliberately slow hashes
description: A unique random salt per password gives identical passwords different hashes and defeats precomputed tables; password hashes are deliberately slow so stolen hashes are costly to guess; NIST requires salted, iterated hashing.

facts.text: A salt is a unique random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables of hashes stop working.
Fast hashes let attackers test huge numbers of guesses quickly, so password hashing uses deliberately slow algorithms.
NIST requires sites to store passwords salted and hashed.

title: Each character multiplies the guesses
description: Each extra character multiplies the possible passwords by the number of symbols it could be; offline attackers compute billions of hashes per second, so length is a primary factor, but common and leaked passwords are tried first.

facts.text: A 4-digit passcode has 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 possibilities, so a 5-digit one has 100,000; four letters from 52 upper- and lowercase letters give 52 x 52 x 52 x 52, over 7 million.
Thieves who steal hashed passwords can guess offline, with no login page limiting attempts, computing many billions of hashes per second.
NIST calls password length a primary factor in password strength.
Attackers try dictionary words and passwords leaked in earlier breaches, which is why NIST says sites should block them.
CISA advises a different password for every account, such as a passphrase of 4 to 7 unrelated words, kept in a password manager.

title: One reused password, many doors
description: Credential stuffing tries username and password pairs leaked from one site on other sites, so a reused password lets one breach open many accounts.

facts.text: Credential stuffing takes username and password pairs leaked from one website and tries them on other websites.

title: A second factor
description: Multifactor authentication asks for two or more kinds of proof (know, have, are), so a stolen password alone fails; codes can still be phished, and CISA ranks text or email codes weakest and security keys best.

facts.text: Multifactor authentication asks for two or more kinds of proof: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or security key) or something you are (a fingerprint or face).
With MFA on, someone who has stolen your password still cannot get in without the second factor.

A fake login page can collect your password and the 6-digit code from your phone together and pass them on; CISA ranks text or email codes the weakest MFA and security keys the best against phishing, though any MFA beats none.

title: Passkeys
description: A passkey is a key pair: the private key stays on your device and the site stores only the public key; it is bound to the real site, so look-alike pages get nothing and breaches leak no password.

facts.text: A passkey is a pair of keys: the private key stays on your device, the website stores only the public key, and you unlock it the way you unlock your device.
Passkeys are cryptographically bound to the real website, so a look-alike site cannot use them, and there is no password on the server to steal.

title: Public and private keys
description: Public-key cryptography publishes one key and keeps its partner secret: what the public key locks only the private key unlocks, so strangers need no shared secret first. Found in 1976 publicly and earlier in secret at GCHQ.

facts.text: In public-key cryptography each user publishes one key and keeps its partner secret; a message locked with the public key can be unlocked only with the matching private key.
Diffie and Hellman's 1976 paper showed how people could communicate secretly over an open channel with no prearranged secret.
At Britain's GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson worked out public-key methods earlier in the 1970s, but the work stayed classified until 1997.

title: One-way math and session keys
description: RSA (1977) is safe because multiplying two huge primes is easy but factoring the product is beyond computers; public-key math is slow, so it mainly sets up a session key for faster shared-key encryption.

facts.text: RSA, introduced in 1977 by MIT's Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, multiplies two huge prime numbers; working back from the product to the primes is far beyond computers, which keeps the private key private.
Public-key encryption is slow, so it is mainly used to exchange a session key, which faster shared-key encryption then uses for the data.

title: HTTPS and certificates
description: HTTPS is web traffic secured by TLS: a handshake sets up a session key, then everything is encrypted and tamper-checked; a certificate signed by a certificate authority binds the site's public key to its domain after the CA checks domain control.

facts.text: HTTPS is ordinary web traffic secured by TLS, which encrypts data in transit, detects tampering and lets the server prove who it is.
In the TLS handshake the browser and server agree on a secret key, then use it to encrypt every message, headers included.
A site's certificate holds a digitally signed copy of its public key, tying the key to its domain name; the signer is a certificate authority that browsers trust.
A certificate authority issues a certificate only after the applicant proves it controls the domain, for example by posting a file or a DNS record the authority asks for.

title: What the padlock does not promise
description: The padlock means a private, checked connection to whoever controls that exact domain; certificates are free and only check domain control, and the FBI warns phishing sites use HTTPS too.

facts.text: Let's Encrypt, a widely used nonprofit certificate authority, issues certificates for free.
The FBI warns that https and the lock icon do not mean a site is legitimate: phishing sites use certificates too.

title: Viruses, worms and trojans
description: A virus attaches to other programs and runs when they run; a worm is self-contained and spreads across networks with no host or user action; a trojan looks useful and hides a harmful function you launch yourself.

facts.text: A virus copies itself by attaching to other programs or files, and runs when the infected program is run.
A worm is a self-contained program that spreads itself across networks without a host program or any user action.
A Trojan horse is a program that seems useful but hides a harmful function, which runs when you launch it.
In Greek legend, warriors hid inside a wooden horse to get into Troy, a story told in the Odyssey.

title: Why worms spread fast
description: Worms need no click: they travel through security holes that updates fix. The 1988 Morris worm hit about 6,000 of the internet's 60,000 hosts.

facts.text: Worms move from computer to computer through holes in security, the kind automatic updates fix.
In 1988 the Morris worm caused major problems for about 6,000 of the 60,000 computers then linked to the internet.

title: How ransomware squeezes victims
description: Ransomware encrypts files and sells back the key; organisations that cannot work without their data (hospitals, pipelines) feel the most pressure; gangs also threaten to leak data; the FBI does not support paying.

facts.text: Ransomware encrypts the files on a device, making them and the systems that rely on them unusable, and the attackers demand payment to unlock them.
Ransomware can leave organisations unable to reach the data they need to operate and deliver critical services.
NHS England estimated that over 19,000 appointments were cancelled because of WannaCry.
After a ransomware attack on May 7, 2021, Colonial Pipeline, which carries about 45% of the gasoline used on the US East Coast, halted fuel for nearly a week and paid a $4.4 million ransom.
Ransomware gangs also steal data and threaten to publish it unless the victim pays.
The FBI does not support paying a ransom: payment does not guarantee the data comes back and encourages more attacks.

title: Offline backups beat ransom
description: Keep backups offline, encrypted and tested, because ransomware hunts for any backup it can reach and deletes or encrypts it.

facts.text: CISA advises keeping offline, encrypted backups and testing them regularly, because ransomware tries to find and delete or encrypt any backups it can reach.

title: Phishing hacks the human
description: Social engineering tricks people into revealing information such as passwords; phishing does it with messages and fake sites that pose as trusted organisations, pulling levers like authority, urgency, emotion, scarcity and current events.

facts.text: Social engineering is an attempt to trick someone into revealing information, such as a password, that can be used to attack systems.
Phishing uses emails, messages or malicious websites that pose as a trustworthy organisation to get personal information; it is a form of social engineering.
The UK National Cyber Security Centre lists five tricks scammers use: authority, urgency, emotion, scarcity and current events.

title: Breaking the rush
description: Verify an odd request by contacting the organisation with details you already have, never those in the message; passkeys tied to the real site defeat even perfect fake pages.

facts.text: CISA advises checking a suspicious request by contacting the company directly, using contact details you already have rather than any in the message.

title: Four habits that block most attacks
description: CISA's Secure Our World steps: recognize and report phishing, use strong passwords, turn on MFA, update software, because software flaws can give criminals access to files or accounts.

facts.text: CISA's Secure Our World campaign names four steps: recognize and report phishing, use strong passwords, turn on multifactor authentication, and update software.
CISA warns that flaws in software can give criminals access to files or accounts, so updates should not be delayed.

title: Databases: tables, records and types
description: A database is data organized for fast search and retrieval; a relational database keeps it in tables whose rows are records and whose columns are fields, each column with a data type that gives the stored values their meaning.

facts.text: A database is a collection of data specially organized for rapid search and retrieval by a computer.
Relational databases, the most popular model, store data in tables of rows and columns, much like a spreadsheet.
In a database table each row is one record and each column is a field of that record; the columns are fixed while the number of rows varies.
Each column has a data type, such as whole numbers, text or dates, which limits what it can hold and gives the stored data its meaning so it can be computed with.

title: How an index finds one record
description: Without an index a database must scan every row; an index keeps a column's values sorted, each pointing to its row, like a book's index, at the cost of updating it on every change.

facts.text: Without an index, a database must scan the entire table, row by row, to find matching records.
A database index works like the index at the back of a book: look up the term and go straight to the right page instead of reading everything.
An index keeps one column's values in sorted order, each pointing to the row that holds it, so searching the index is much faster than searching the table.
Every change to a table must also update its indexes, which adds work, so indexes that are rarely used are removed.

title: The data trail a phone leaves
description: A phone works out its location from GPS, Wi-Fi, cell towers and Bluetooth; carriers log each cell-site connection; photos can carry location coordinates; apps and websites track you with advertising IDs and cookies.

facts.text: A phone works out its location from GPS, Wi-Fi networks, cell towers and Bluetooth.
Apps must ask before using your location, and you can allow it only once or only while the app is in use; newer Android phones can share just an approximate location.

Phones continuously connect to cell sites, and each connection creates a time-stamped record that carriers keep; in a 2018 US Supreme Court case such records gave 12,898 location points over 127 days, about 101 a day.
With location turned on for the camera, a phone embeds the coordinates of where a photo or video was taken into the file itself.
When you use a phone app, advertisers may track you with a unique advertising identifier.
Websites may use cookies to recognize you and track your activity even after you leave the site.

title: Metadata: the envelope
description: Metadata is data about data: for a call, the numbers, time and length but not the words. A 2016 Stanford study of 823 volunteers showed call metadata alone can reveal sensitive facts such as a heart condition.

facts.text: Metadata is data about data: information describing data, such as a file's format, rather than its contents.
Phone metadata records the numbers, times and lengths of calls and texts, not what was said.
In a Stanford study published in 2016, researchers collected the call and text logs of 823 volunteers.
From calls to a cardiology group, a pharmacy and a hotline for a heart-rhythm monitoring device, the Stanford researchers inferred that one volunteer likely had a cardiac arrhythmia.
Telephone metadata can reveal where people are, who they are close to and highly sensitive traits.
Encrypting a message's contents doesn't hide that two people are communicating, or when, where and for how long.

title: Why free services show ads
description: Many free services are paid for by advertisers; in 2024 about 98% of Meta's revenue came from ads, and an FTC staff report found business models that encouraged mass data collection for targeted ads.

facts.text: In 2024 Meta's advertising revenue was $160.6 billion of its $164.5 billion total revenue, about 98%.
Companies can show you personalized ads based on your browsing history or your location.

A 2024 FTC staff report on nine large social media and video streaming services found that many of their business models encouraged mass collection of user data to make money, especially through targeted ads.
The FTC staff saw that incentive as in tension with user privacy, and two of the five commissioners filed partly dissenting statements.

title: Ad code inside apps
description: Apps show ads by building in an ad company's software development kit (SDK), which can collect data such as IP address, taps and the advertising ID; app stores make developers declare what their SDKs collect.

facts.text: An app can include a software development kit, or SDK, which is ready-made code from another company, such as an ad network's kit for showing ads.
Google's mobile ads SDK says it automatically collects a phone's IP address (to estimate general location), taps and other app interactions, and the advertising ID.
Google Play requires app makers to declare data collected by the SDKs in their app as part of the app's own data safety disclosures.

title: Data brokers
description: Data brokers collect details about people from many sources without their knowledge, combine them into profiles and segments (3,000 per person at one broker the FTC studied in 2014) and sell them; the FTC has acted against a broker selling sensitive location data.

facts.text: Data brokers collect information from public records such as voter registrations, purchase data, web browsing and warranty registrations, not from consumers directly.
