Because data brokers don't get the data from consumers, most people are largely unaware it is being collected and used.
Each source may give a broker only a few details, but put together they form a detailed picture of a person's life, which brokers sell for purposes such as marketing and fraud detection.
In its 2014 study of nine data brokers, the FTC found that one had 3,000 data segments for nearly every US consumer.
Brokers sort people into segments, categories such as 'Expectant Parent', 'Diabetes Interest' and 'Cholesterol Focus', some of which guess at sensitive matters like health.

In 2024 the FTC barred broker X-Mode Social and successor Outlogic from selling sensitive location data, alleging it sold precise locations, gathered via its apps and code in others, that could reveal visits to clinics, worship places and shelters.
X-Mode Social settled the FTC's allegations without admitting wrongdoing.

title: Anonymous data that isn't
description: Removing names doesn't make data anonymous: Sweeney matched ZIP code, birth date and sex in 'anonymous' health data to a $20 voter list and found Governor Weld's record, and estimated 87% of Americans are likely unique on those three details.

facts.text: Massachusetts' Group Insurance Commission collected health records for about 135,000 state employees and their families and, believing them anonymous, gave copies to researchers and sold a copy to industry.

Latanya Sweeney bought the Cambridge, Massachusetts voter list for twenty dollars; it held each voter's name, address, ZIP code, birth date and sex, and the health data held the same ZIP code, birth date and sex.
Governor William Weld's record was in the health data: six Cambridge voters shared his birth date, only three were men, and only he lived in his ZIP code.
Sweeney estimated that 87% of the US population was likely unique on just ZIP code, birth date and sex.
In the Cambridge voter list, 2 sexes, 5 ZIP codes and birth dates spread over 365 days and 100 years gave 365,000 possible combinations, for only 54,805 voters.
The more details a dataset reports about a person, the more likely they combine to identify that person, especially when linked to another dataset that has names.

title: The 2017 Equifax breach
description: A known Apache Struts flaw went unpatched on Equifax's dispute portal; attackers entered in May 2017, used unencrypted passwords to reach 48 more databases, ran about 9,000 queries over about 76 days and exposed data on about 147 million people.

facts.text: In 2017, the Equifax data breach exposed the personal information of about 147 million people.
In March 2017 a flaw in Apache Struts web software was publicly announced, but the fix was not installed on Equifax's online dispute portal.
In May 2017 attackers used the flaw to break into the dispute portal and began extracting personal data.
The attackers ran about 9,000 database queries, and the attack lasted about 76 days before it was discovered.
The intrusion was discovered in July 2017, and Equifax announced the breach in September 2017.
Inside, the attackers found usernames and passwords stored unencrypted, which let them reach 48 more databases beyond the portal's 3.
The attackers took names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers, sending the data out in small encrypted pieces that looked like normal traffic.

title: Defenses that shrink a breach
description: Services should store passwords only as salted hashes (NIST), multi-factor authentication stops a stolen password alone from working (CISA), and a free credit freeze blocks new credit in your name (FTC).

facts.text: NIST's guidelines require services to store passwords salted and hashed, a one-way scrambling, so a stolen copy can't simply be read back.
With multi-factor authentication, an attacker who steals one factor, like a password, still can't meet the second requirement.
In the US, placing a credit freeze is free and stops new credit accounts from being opened in your name.

title: End-to-end encryption
description: With end-to-end encryption only the sender and recipient hold the keys, so the service can't read messages; transport encryption lets the service see copies. Keys are strings of bits (AES uses 128, 192 or 256), and encryption doesn't hide metadata.

facts.text: With transport-layer encryption, messages are locked from your device to the service's servers and on to the recipient, but the service can see unencrypted copies in the middle.
With end-to-end encryption, a message is locked by the sender and unlocked only by the recipient; only the two ends hold the keys, so the service can't read it.
The AES encryption standard uses keys 128, 192 or 256 bits long.
Because each added bit doubles the number of possible patterns, each added bit of key length doubles the number of possible keys.
Encryption doesn't hide that two people are communicating, or the times, location and length of their communication.

title: The lawful access debate
description: Law enforcement officials call strong end-to-end encryption warrant-proof and want lawful access; security experts argue any door that a key can open adds a vulnerability; as of a January 2024 CRS report, no lawful-only door had been demonstrated.

facts.text: Law enforcement officials call strong end-to-end encryption 'warrant-proof', because companies that don't hold the keys can't decrypt messages even for a search warrant.
Security experts argue that any built-in door that a key can open, whoever holds the key, adds a weakness criminals and other attackers could exploit.
As of a January 2024 congressional research report, researchers had not shown how to build a door that could be opened only in lawful circumstances.

title: What the GDPR lets you ask
description: The EU's GDPR (applied from 25 May 2018) gives rights of access, correction, erasure and portability in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, with answers due within one month and fines up to 20 million euros or 4% of turnover.

facts.text: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation has applied since 25 May 2018.
The GDPR lets you get a copy of the personal data a company holds on you, have inaccurate data corrected and, in many cases, have it erased.
Under the GDPR, a company must answer a person's request without undue delay and at the latest within one month.
The most serious GDPR breaches can bring fines of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide yearly turnover, whichever is higher.
The GDPR's right to data portability lets you receive the data you gave a company in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and pass it to another service.
Britain's data regulator, the ICO, names CSV, a standard format for spreadsheet data, as one format that meets the portability rule.

title: What California's privacy law lets you ask
description: California's Consumer Privacy Act (in effect from 2020, expanded from 2023) gives the rights to know, delete, correct, limit sensitive data and opt out of sale or sharing, with most requests answered within 45 calendar days.

facts.text: California's Consumer Privacy Act took effect in 2020, and amendments expanding it began on January 1, 2023.

California's privacy law gives residents the right to know what a business collected about them, to have it deleted or corrected, to limit use of sensitive information and to tell the business to stop selling or sharing it.
Under California's privacy law, businesses must respond to requests to know, delete or correct within 45 calendar days.

title: How offline data follows you online
description: Data brokers use websites with sign-up features and cookies to recognize people online and target ads to them based on what they did offline, joining the separate pieces of a person's data trail.

facts.text: Data brokers use websites with registration features and cookies to find people online and target internet ads to them based on their offline activities.

title: Dijkstra's shortest-path search
description: A road map becomes a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's algorithm grows outward from the start, always expanding the unvisited place with the smallest known distance.

facts.text: Edsger Dijkstra conceived his shortest-path algorithm in about twenty minutes over coffee on a cafe terrace in Amsterdam, used it in 1956 to show off the new ARMAC computer, and published it in 1959.

A road network can be stored as a weighted graph: intersections are nodes, roads between them are edges, and each edge carries a weight, the cost of travelling it, such as driving time. The best route is the path with the smallest total weight.

Dijkstra's algorithm starts the source at distance 0, then repeatedly takes the unvisited node with the smallest known distance and updates its neighbors' distances when it finds a shorter path, until the destination is selected.

title: Live traffic in route finding
description: Map apps keep updating road weights with live and predicted traffic, and switch routes when a jam is predicted.

facts.text: Google Maps uses aggregate location data from people navigating to understand current traffic, and combines it with historical traffic patterns for each road, using machine learning to predict traffic later in a drive.
If Google Maps predicts that traffic is likely to become heavy on a route, it automatically finds a lower-traffic alternative.

title: Collaborative filtering
description: Recommenders suggest what people with overlapping tastes liked, using only their ratings and choices; the Netflix Prize paid for better rating predictions.

facts.text: In October 2006 Netflix offered $1 million to anyone who could make its Cinematch recommendation system 10 percent more accurate.

Recommenders rest on the idea that if two people enjoy the same things, they are likely to share other favorites; collaborative filtering recommends an item to one user based on the interests of a similar user.
Collaborative filtering needs no knowledge about the items themselves: it can learn from users' feedback alone.
The Netflix Prize data were star ratings, from one to five, that Netflix customers gave to movies; algorithms used them to predict the ratings people would give films they had not rated.

In September 2009 the $1 million Netflix Prize went to BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, a merger of teams; its final entry and the runner-up's were a mathematical tie, and the team that submitted first won.

title: The cold-start problem
description: A collaborative filter cannot recommend a brand-new item that nobody has rated, because it has no overlap to go on.

facts.text: A collaborative filtering system cannot handle fresh items: if nobody has interacted with a new item yet, the system has nothing to learn it from. This is called the cold-start problem.

title: Engagement-ranked feeds
description: Social feeds score each post by predicted reactions and sort by that score instead of by time.

facts.text: Instagram's feed was a single chronological stream when it launched in 2010; by 2016 people were missing 70% of the posts in their feeds, and Instagram introduced a feed ranked by what people care about.

Facebook describes Feed ranking in steps: gather the inventory of posts you could see, consider thousands of signals, make personalized predictions, then calculate a relevance score for each post and put posts in order by that score.
One of the signals Instagram uses is your history of interacting with someone, such as whether you comment on each other's posts.

Instagram says the five interactions its Feed ranking watches most closely are how likely you are to spend a few seconds on a post, comment on it, like it, reshare it and tap the profile photo; the more likely and the more heavily weighted, the higher the post.
Facebook's Feeds tab, launched in 2022, shows the newest posts first, sorted in reverse chronological order.

title: Real-time bidding for ads
description: While a page loads, its ad space is auctioned: a bid request describing the viewer goes out, bidders reply within a deadline, and the highest bid wins.

facts.text: As a website loads, its publisher can auction ad space on the page; advertisers bid, the process can involve many companies and happens in milliseconds, and billions of online ads are placed this way every day.
A bid request commonly includes the user's IP address, cookie IDs, the browser and device type, the user's location, time zone and language.
On Google's ad exchange, a bidder typically gets 80 to 1,000 milliseconds to answer a bid request; late responses are excluded, and the highest bid wins the ad space.

In 2019 the UK's data protection regulator, the ICO, reported that bid requests normally contain personal data and that many participants in real-time bidding were engaging with it without fully understanding the privacy issues.

title: How spam filters learn
description: A spam filter learns which words and signals predict junk by counting them in labeled piles of spam and good mail, and keeps learning from new reports.

facts.text: In his 2002 essay 'A Plan for Spam', Paul Graham reported that his statistical filter found 'ff0000', the web code for bright red, to be as good an indicator of spam as any rude word.

Graham's filter starts with one pile of spam and one of good mail, counts how often each word appears in each pile, turns the counts into the probability that an email containing the word is spam, and scores a new email by combining its most telling words' probabilities.
Supervised learning trains a model on labeled examples so it learns which features predict the label; identifying spam is a standard example.
Graham argued each user should have a delete-as-spam button feeding their own spam pile; Gmail says that as you report more spam, it identifies similar emails as spam more efficiently.
Spam keeps changing, and statistical filters that learn from new mail evolve with it.

title: Batched rider-driver matching
description: Ride apps pair riders and drivers in batches to cut the average wait for everyone, because the closest car is not always the quickest.

facts.text: Uber says it first matched riders by asking 'Who's closest?' but learned that closest doesn't always mean quickest, because traffic, overpasses and rivers add complexity.
In the seconds after a rider requests a ride, Uber evaluates nearby drivers and riders in one batch and pairs them to reduce the average wait time for everyone, not just the closest pair.

title: Surge pricing
description: When ride requests outnumber drivers in an area, prices rise in real time to draw drivers in and shift demand; emergencies are capped.

facts.text: Uber's surge pricing goes into effect when there are more riders in an area than available drivers, as in bad weather, rush hour or special events; surge rates update in real time and differ between neighborhoods.
Higher surge prices are meant to encourage more drivers to serve the busy area and to shift rider demand, since some riders choose to wait for prices to fall.
In July 2014 Uber agreed with New York's attorney general to cap its prices during emergencies and natural disasters, in line with the state's price-gouging law, and the rules applied nationally.

title: Hash-matching known images
description: Moderation systems catch copies of already-identified images by comparing image fingerprints against a database.

facts.text: PhotoDNA, developed by Microsoft with Dartmouth College starting in 2009, creates a digital signature, or hash, of an image and compares it with the signatures of images already identified as illegal to find copies.

title: Moderation mistakes at scale
description: Automated systems flag and humans review, but context is hard and even a small error rate means many wrong calls at millions of decisions a day.

facts.text: Meta said in January 2025 that in December 2024 it removed millions of pieces of content every day, and that it thought one to two out of every 10 of those actions may have been mistakes.

Meta says its technology detects most violating content before anyone reports it, and sends potentially violating content to review teams, thousands of reviewers around the world, to check and take action.
Context changes meaning: the same words can be a slur in one post and mean something else in another, so reviewers must judge context.

In September 2016 Facebook removed posts of 'The Terror of War', the Vietnam War photo of a naked girl fleeing a napalm attack, then reinstated it after a global outcry, citing its history and global importance.

title: Feedback loops in recommenders
description: A recommender learns from clicks it helped cause, which can amplify popularity and make behavior more alike.

facts.text: In an experiment run in 2004 and 2005 and published in 2006, Salganik, Dodds and Watts let people download songs by unknown bands; people in eight independent worlds could see each song's download count in their own world, and this social influence made success more unequal and less predictable.
In that experiment success was only partly determined by quality: the best songs rarely did poorly and the worst rarely did well, but any other result was possible.
Recommendation systems are often trained on data from users who were already shown algorithmic recommendations, which creates a feedback loop.
Recommenders tend to show a few popular items often while most items are ignored, and the loop of recommending, reacting and retraining can amplify this popularity bias.
Simulations by Chaney and colleagues showed that training on data shaped by earlier recommendations can make users' behavior more alike without making them better off.

title: Auditing algorithms from outside
description: Auditors read code when they can, and otherwise test a system with chosen inputs, as the 2018 Gender Shades audit did.

facts.text: Researchers can audit an algorithm by reading its code when it is public, or from outside by sending repeated queries and observing the results, or by running programmed fake users called sock puppets.

In 2018 Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested three commercial gender classification systems on 1,270 faces balanced by gender and skin type, and found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women but at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.

title: Rights over automated decisions
description: The GDPR limits decisions made solely by automated processing and gives rights to a human and to information; New York City requires bias audits of hiring tools.

facts.text: GDPR Article 22 gives a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; where one is allowed because it is needed for a contract or rests on explicit consent, people keep at least the right to human intervention, to give a view and to contest it.
The GDPR also gives people the right to meaningful information about the logic involved in such automated decision-making.

New York City's Local Law 144 of 2021 bars employers from using an automated employment decision tool unless it has had a bias audit within one year before use, a summary of the results is public and candidates are notified; enforcement began July 5, 2023.

title: Every chooser chases a number
description: Route finders, ride matchers, feeds, ad auctions and spam filters each pick by optimizing a number: travel time, average wait, predicted reactions, bid price or spam probability.

facts.text: Each choosing algorithm in this chapter optimizes a number: route finders the smallest total travel time, ride matchers the lowest average wait, feeds a score from predicted reactions, ad auctions the highest bid, spam filters a spam probability.

title: Rules or examples
description: Classic software follows rules a person writes; machine learning trains a model on examples. Learning wins when the patterns are too many to write down; rules win when they can be stated exactly.

facts.text: Arthur Samuel's checkers program at IBM recorded each position it saw and whether it led to a win or a loss, so it got better the more games it played.
Samuel called this process machine learning, a term he coined.
In 1959 Samuel reported that a computer can be programmed to learn to play a better game of checkers than the person who wrote the program.
In machine learning, software called a model is trained on data to make predictions; its logic is learned from examples rather than written as explicit rules.
As tasks get more complex, rule-based systems become brittle, because it is often impossible to write down every pattern and variable that matters.
Machine learning requires data; Google's rules for ML engineering advise not being afraid to launch a product without machine learning.
Google's guide advises checking for a non-ML solution first: ML needs dedicated long-term maintenance, and the non-ML solution is the benchmark an ML solution must beat.

title: Training, testing and overfitting
description: A model is judged on a held-back test set of examples it never saw; an overfit model memorized its training set and fails on new data.

facts.text: Data for machine learning is usually split into a training set the model learns from, a validation set for checks during training, and a test set to judge the trained model.
The only fair test of a model is against new examples, so test examples that duplicate training examples should be deleted.
Overfitting means a model matches, or memorizes, its training set so closely that it fails to make correct predictions on new data.
A low error rate on the training data combined with a high error rate on the test data signals overfitting.
A model that makes good predictions on new data generalizes well, the opposite of overfitting.
If each pixel is one bit (black or white), a 20-pixel picture has 2 to the 20th power, or 1,048,576, possible patterns, since each added bit doubles the count.

title: How a neural network learns
description: Neurons in layers multiply inputs by weights and add them up; training measures the error and nudges every weight a little to shrink it.

facts.text: A neural network stacks simple artificial neurons in layers: an input layer, hidden layers, and an output layer that produces the prediction.
Each neuron multiplies each of its inputs by a weight, adds the results and adds a bias; these weights and biases are the parameters the network learns.
Training repeats a loop: calculate the loss (how wrong the predictions are), find the direction that reduces it, move the weights a small amount that way, and repeat.
Backpropagation works backward through the network, calculating how much each weight and bias contributed to the error.
In 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams described in Nature how to train a network by back-propagating errors, repeatedly adjusting its weights.
GPT-3, a language model described in 2020, had 175 billion parameters.

title: Why AI runs on graphics chips
description: GPUs run thousands of calculations at once, which suits the multiplications of deep learning; big models need thousands of GPUs and a lot of electricity.

facts.text: Graphics processing units, or GPUs, were originally designed to speed up 3-D graphics rendering.
GPUs run many calculations at the same time on hundreds or even thousands of cores, while CPUs generally work serially, finishing one process before the next.
Deep learning involves huge numbers of matrix calculations, and GPUs' ability to run thousands of them at once makes them far more efficient for it than traditional processors.
A 2021 study estimated that training GPT-3 used 10,000 GPUs for 14.8 days (about 15) and 1,287 megawatt-hours of electricity.
10,000 GPUs for 14.8 days is 148,000 chip-days, about 400 years of work for a single chip.
1,287 megawatt-hours is about what 120 average US homes used in a year in 2022, when a home averaged 10,791 kilowatt-hours.
In 2024, Meta reported training its largest Llama 3 model on up to 16,000 GPUs.

title: Tokens and the next token
description: Text is split into subword tokens, each swapped for a number; a language model scores every token in its vocabulary, picks one, appends it and repeats.

facts.text: Subword tokenizers keep frequent words whole but split rare words into meaningful, more common pieces, such as annoyingly into annoying and ly.
Models can only process numbers, so a tokenizer converts each token into an ID, its number in the model's vocabulary.
GPT-2, from 2019, had a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens.
To choose the next token, a language model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary.
Text is generated one token at a time: each new token is appended and depends on all the tokens before it.
A setting called temperature shapes the pick: higher values make choices more random, lower values more focused and predictable.

title: From predictor to assistant
description: A pretrained next-token predictor is fine-tuned on human-written demonstrations, then on human rankings through a reward model (RLHF).

facts.text: Predicting the next token of text from the internet is a different goal from following a user's instructions helpfully and safely, a 2022 paper noted.
In the method, people wrote example answers showing the desired behavior, and the pretrained model was fine-tuned on those demonstrations.
Labelers ranked several model outputs; a reward model trained on those rankings scores text by predicted human preference, and the model is tuned to earn higher scores (RLHF).
In the 2022 tests, people preferred answers from a 1.3 billion-parameter tuned model to those of the 175 billion-parameter GPT-3, despite 100 times fewer parameters.
The labelers were a team of 40 contractors, and the authors noted the model was aligned to a specific group, mostly labelers and researchers, not any broader notion of human values.

title: Why chatbots make things up
description: Language models produce likely text, so they can state falsehoods confidently (confabulation); the check that works is a source outside the chatbot.

facts.text: In the 2023 Mata v. Avianca case, lawyers filed a brief citing court cases ChatGPT had made up; asked by one lawyer whether a case was real, ChatGPT said it existed.
NIST calls it confabulation: generative AI confidently presenting erroneous or false content, colloquially called hallucinations.
NIST says confabulation is a natural result of how generative models work: they produce outputs that approximate the statistical patterns of their training data.
A 2025 paper argued that, like students facing hard exams, models guess when unsure, because training and most evaluations reward guessing over admitting uncertainty.
NIST warns that generative AI can produce confabulated citations that appear to justify its answers.
The lawyer testified that he entered the citation on a free site and couldn't find the decision, yet cited it anyway.

title: Pictures from noise
description: Diffusion models learn to remove noise added step by step to real images, then generate by denoising random noise, steered by a text prompt.

facts.text: To make a new image, a trained diffusion model starts from random noise and removes noise step by step.
To train a diffusion model, images from the training set are turned into pure noise by adding a little noise at each step.
The model learns to reverse this: at each step it predicts the noise in the image and removes a fraction of it.
Text-to-image diffusion models let users steer the output with a text prompt, interpreted by a separate language model.
The influential 2020 diffusion paper by Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel at UC Berkeley used 1,000 steps.
Adding random noise to an image's pixels, step by step, eventually leaves what looks like TV static.

title: Telling real from synthetic
description: People and detectors struggle to spot synthetic media; provenance records such as C2PA Content Credentials can be signed, but are often stripped.

facts.text: In a 2022 study, people told AI-synthesized faces from real ones with 48% accuracy, close to the 50% of chance; after training, 59%.
NIST calls automated detection of synthetic content a cat-and-mouse game: generators improve as detectors appear, and detectors often work best only on generators they trained on.
The C2PA, a coalition of companies and organizations, publishes an open standard that records the origin and edits of digital content, shown as Content Credentials, likened to a nutrition label.
A digital signature on provenance data gives assurance of who signed it and that it was not modified after signing.
Metadata can be stripped from a file, as often happens when files are shared on social media, sometimes to deceive and sometimes for privacy.

title: A model is only its data
description: Everything a model learns arrives as numbers from its examples, so data that is scarce, wrong or unrepresentative makes the model fail.

facts.text: Text reaches a language model as token IDs, images are grids of pixel values, and a network's learning is stored in its weights: all of it is numbers.
Google's guide says data for predictive machine learning should be abundant, reliable, correct and representative.

title: Megabits for speed, megabytes for files
description: Internet speeds are sold in megabits per second (small b); files are measured in megabytes (big B). A byte is 8 bits, so divide a speed by 8 to compare it with a file size.

facts.text: Internet speeds are measured in megabits per second (Mbps, with a lowercase b), while file sizes are counted in megabytes (MB, with an uppercase B).
A byte is 8 bits, so 1 megabyte per second equals 8 megabits per second: divide a speed in Mbps by 8 to get megabytes per second.

title: Working out a real download time
description: Divide the advertised speed by 8 to get megabytes per second, then divide the file size by that. The result is a best case: typical speeds are lower.

facts.text: A 100 Mbps connection moves at most about 12.5 megabytes a second, so a 1 GB (1,000 MB) file takes at least 80 seconds and a 100 MB file at least 8.
Since April 2024, large US internet providers have had to publish a broadband label for each plan listing typical download and upload speeds at peak hours, not just the advertised top speed.

title: What the phone-listening study found
description: A 2018 Northeastern University study of more than 17,000 Android apps found no app secretly switching on the microphone to send audio, but did find apps sending screenshots and screen recordings to other companies.

facts.text: In a 2018 study, Northeastern University researchers tested more than 17,000 popular Android apps and found none secretly switching on the microphone to send audio.
The Northeastern researchers ran the apps with an automated test program and watched what each app sent out.
The same study found apps sending screenshots and screen recordings to other companies without telling the user; one food-delivery app sent its screens to an analytics firm.

title: Why ads can feel like eavesdropping
description: Ads can match your life without a microphone: location from GPS and cell towers, tracking of browsing and shopping, and profiles combined across apps. iPhones show an orange dot when the microphone is in use.

facts.text: Companies can target ads using location tracked by GPS and cell towers, tracking pixels that record what you browse and put in your cart, and profiles combined across many apps.
On an iPhone with iOS 14 or later, an orange dot shows when an app is using the microphone, and a green dot when the camera is in use, with or without the microphone.

title: AI's jagged frontier
description: As of 2026, AI can excel at some very hard tasks (gold-medal olympiad math) while failing some easy ones (reading an analog clock), and its scores change fast, so every claim needs a task and a date.

facts.text: In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal scores at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
The 2026 AI Index found that the best AI model read analog clocks correctly only 50.1% of the time.
Researchers call AI's uneven abilities, excellent at some hard tasks yet unreliable at some easy ones, its jagged frontier.
The 2026 AI Index reports that the top score on a leading coding benchmark rose from about 60% to near 100% in a single year.

title: Confident is not correct
description: NIST lists confabulation (hallucination), confidently stated but false content, as a key risk of generative AI, so an answer's tone is no evidence of its truth.

facts.text: NIST's 2024 Generative AI Profile lists confabulation, confidently stated but erroneous or false content, often called hallucination, as a risk of generative AI.

title: Which encryption quantum computers threaten
description: Shor's 1994 algorithm means a large quantum computer could break public-key methods like RSA and elliptic curves. Symmetric encryption such as AES with 128-bit or longer keys is not significantly affected, but data stored today could be decrypted later.

facts.text: In 1994 Peter Shor devised an algorithm that would let a large enough quantum computer factor huge numbers, breaking encryption built on multiplying two large primes.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre says a large enough quantum computer would break today's public-key methods, including RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
The NCSC says symmetric encryption is not significantly affected by quantum computers: algorithms such as AES with keys of at least 128 bits can still be used.
The NCSC warns that attackers could collect encrypted data today and store it, planning to decrypt it once a quantum computer exists.

title: Post-quantum standards
description: NIST released its first three post-quantum encryption standards on August 13, 2024, urged organizations to switch now, and plans to remove quantum-vulnerable algorithms from its standards by 2035.

facts.text: On August 13, 2024, NIST released its first three finalized encryption standards designed to withstand attack by a quantum computer, and urged organizations to start switching immediately.
NIST said in 2024 that some experts predict a quantum computer able to break current encryption could appear within a decade.
NIST plans to deprecate and then remove quantum-vulnerable algorithms from its standards by 2035.

title: The dot-com boom and bust
description: Money poured into overvalued internet start-ups in the late 1990s; the Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 and lost more than three quarters of its value by October 2002, and firms like Pets.com went bust.

facts.text: The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose quickly from 1995, peaked on March 10, 2000, and by October 2002 had lost more than three quarters of its value.
Many dot-com start-ups were overvalued, often with little to show in the way of a product.
A bubble is when an asset's price stays far above what its fundamentals justify, as buyers pay more hoping to sell to someone more optimistic.

Pets.com, known for its sock-puppet mascot, went public in February 2000 and shut down in November 2000; by the end of September 2000 it had lost about $147 million since it started, about $85 million of that in 2000's first nine months.
By the end of 2001 most dot-com stocks, such as Pets.com, Webvan and eToys, had gone bust, although some companies survived.

title: Real technology, hyped prices
description: The dot-com crash wiped out share prices, not the internet: by 2024 about 5.5 billion people were online. Judge hype by splitting two questions: is the technology real, and is the price sensible?

facts.text: The ITU estimates that about 5.5 billion people, 68% of the world's population, were online in 2024.

title: Moore's law is a prediction
description: Moore predicted in 1965 that transistors per chip would double yearly, revised in 1975 to every two years: an industry observation, not physics. In 2022 two chip-company chiefs disagreed on whether it had ended.

facts.text: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted the number of transistors on a chip would double every year; in 1975 he revised it to every two years. It is a prediction, not a law of physics.
Moore's prediction set expectations for the chip industry and became a target it worked to meet.
In September 2022, Nvidia's chief executive said Moore's law was dead, while Intel's chief executive said it was alive and well.

title: Faster without faster clocks
description: Clock rates stopped climbing in the mid-2000s because more speed cost too much power and heat, so chips added cores; as transistors near their size limit, gains come from software, algorithms and specialized hardware.

facts.text: Processor clock rates climbed for years, then stopped climbing in the mid-2000s, because extra speed was no longer worth the power it used and the heat it made.
Chipmakers turned to multiple cores: two cores at 80% of the clock rate give 73% more performance for the same power, by Intel's rule of thumb.
MIT researchers wrote in 2020 that transistors are nearing the limit of how small they can get, so gains must come from software, algorithms and hardware design.
Hardware customized for particular jobs can be much more efficient than general-purpose chips, the MIT researchers wrote.

title: What open source means
description: Open-source software comes with its source code and lets anyone share, sell, change and pass on changed versions; closed-source software publishes only the finished program and keeps its source code secret.

facts.text: Under the Open Source Definition, open-source software must come with its source code, and its license must let anyone give it away or sell it, change it, and share changed versions.
Closed-source software publishes only the finished program, the object code, and keeps its human-readable source code secret.

title: Open vs. closed: the trade-offs
description: Open code can be inspected and kept alive by anyone but may depend on volunteers (Log4j, 2021); closed software depends on its maker's support decisions (Windows 10's end of support in 2025).

facts.text: In November 2021 an outside security engineer reported a critical flaw in Log4j, open-source software very broadly used in services, websites and apps; it could let an attacker take control of a system.
A US review board found in 2022 that open-source projects like Log4j generally rely on volunteer teams without dedicated security resources.
Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025: its PCs still work but no longer get security updates, except through an extended program running to October 2027.

title: Data-center electricity, measured and forecast
description: The IEA estimates data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity), most of it for servers; forecasts are scenario ranges, and estimates vary partly because data is patchy.

facts.text: The IEA estimates that data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of the world's electricity.
About 60% of a data center's electricity powers its servers; cooling takes from about 7% in efficient hyperscale centers to over 30% in less efficient ones.
There is no federal registration requirement for data centers in the US, so even estimates of how many there are vary by source.

title: Why the energy bill is growing
description: The IEA's 2025 report projects data-center use more than doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver; a 2024 Berkeley Lab report put US data centers at 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and 6.7% to 12% by 2028.

facts.text: The IEA's 2025 Energy and AI report projects data-center electricity use more than doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today, with AI the most important driver.
A 2024 Berkeley Lab report for the US Energy Department found data centers used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, with scenarios of 6.7% to 12% by 2028.

title: What a VPN really does
description: A VPN encrypts your traffic to the VPN company's server, hiding it from your internet or Wi-Fi provider but not from the VPN provider: it moves trust rather than removing it.

facts.text: A VPN routes your traffic through an encrypted tunnel to the VPN's server, hiding it from your internet provider or public Wi-Fi but leaving it visible to the VPN provider.

title: Three questions for any tech claim
description: Test a tech claim with three questions: how does it work, who says so, and what does it cost you in money, data or trust.

facts.text: The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights nonprofit, says a VPN is not a tool for anonymity, because companies have many other ways to track you.
Some free VPNs make money by selling their users' data, EFF warns, and the FTC advises checking whether a VPN app shares your information with third parties.
